3925.event: The Ship of Dreams is the film Titanic, released in December 1997. Directed by James Cameron, the three hour romance set aboard the doomed liner became the highest earning film ever made up to that time, passing every record before it. Audiences wept in packed theaters, returned to watch it again, and made its love theme one of the most played songs in the world. It won eleven Academy Awards, tying the all time record. The film did for 1912 what no history book had done: it put millions of living people aboard the ship, made them love two young passengers, and then made them watch the ocean take them. The ship of dreams sailed into history twice.
3925.announce: Here is a poem about the film that made the whole world weep for 1912: The Ship of Dreams.
3925.title: The Ship of Dreams
3925.piece:
Cameron built the ship again,
three hours long, and filled it with the young,
and the world went aboard and wept for 1912.
I saw it twice in the opening week,
the crowd around me sobbing at the stern.
The ship of dreams sailed into box office history,
the biggest film the world had ever seen.
A poor boy shouts from the bow that he is king of the world.
A poor girl lets the cold sea keep her heart.
Love stories, it turns out,
can float even the heaviest ships.

3944.event: The Night the Computers Didn't Break is the story of the Y2K scare, which ended on January 1, 2000. For years, experts had warned that computer systems storing years as two digits would fail when the calendar rolled from 99 to 00, reading 2000 as 1900. Banks, airlines, power grids, and governments spent vast sums rewriting code and testing systems. Survivalists stocked food. Preachers named the date. Then midnight came, the clocks turned over, and almost nothing happened. A few minor glitches flickered and died. Humanity had spent billions preparing for an apocalypse and bought itself an ordinary New Year. It remains the most expensive scare that never happened, and proof that preparation works.
3944.announce: A poem about the midnight that arrived like any other midnight: The Night the Computers Didn't Break.
3944.title: The Night the Computers Didn't Break
3944.piece:
They told us the world would end at midnight,
every banker, every coder, every screen gone dark,
the planes would fall, the lights go out,
because some tired programmer wrote the year with two digits.
I walked the server rooms and saw the fear,
the money spent, the keyboards worn to bone.
Then the clock turned over, clean and clear,
and nothing broke at all. We had outgrown
our own small prophecy of doom that year.
The costliest fix in history, and it worked.
Sometimes the end of the world we prepare for
is only the shadow of the work we did.
